note: Original illustrative healthcare cases developed from the reviewed course scope. No teacher questions or datasets are reproduced. Topic 6 remains additional, time permitting.

cases.title: Describe a ward’s observed stays
cases.scenario: Eight illustrative hospital stays are 1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 6, 10 and 12 days. Describe these admissions using the slide np percentile convention. These observations are an example, not a random-sampling claim about every hospital.
cases.focus: Ordering, centre, quartile convention and shape

fields.label: Mean stay (days)
fields.hint: Sum all eight stays, then divide by 8.

fields.label: Median stay (days)
fields.hint: Average the fourth and fifth ordered values.

fields.label: IQR, slide np convention (days)
fields.hint: For Q1 use positions 2 and 3; for Q3 use positions 6 and 7.

steps.title: Define the unit
steps.text: The statistical unit is an admission; length of stay is a quantitative variable measured in days. Repeated admissions by the same person would need care in a later independence claim.

steps.title: Find the centre
steps.text: The sum is 40, so x̄=40/8=5 days. The median is (3+4)/2=3.5 days. The mode is 2 days.

steps.title: Name the percentile rule
steps.text: With the slide np rule, Q1=(2+2)/2=2 and Q3=(6+10)/2=8, giving IQR=6 days. Excel QUARTILE.INC instead gives Q1=2, Q3=7 and IQR=5.

steps.title: Interpret shape and flags
steps.text: The longer stays extend the right tail. The slide-rule fences are −7 and 17 days; no observed stay is outside them. A negative lower fence is a mathematical threshold, not a possible hospital stay.

cases.reflection: Write a two-sentence summary for a ward manager. Explain why Excel may give a different IQR.
cases.model: Among these eight observed admissions, the mean stay is 5 days and the median is 3.5 days, with a right tail reaching 12 days. The middle-half spread is 6 days under the slide np convention; Excel’s inclusive interpolation gives 5 days. These are sample descriptions, not evidence of a population change.
rubric: Names admissions and reports centre with units
Explains the right tail without deleting long stays
Names the quartile convention and limits the claim to observed data
cases.trap: Do not mark an Excel IQR of 5 as an arithmetic error if the question uses QUARTILE.INC. State which convention answers the question.

cases.title: One long stay changes the story
cases.scenario: Five observed stays are 2, 4, 4, 5 and 10 days. A corrected record changes the final stay from 10 to 30 days, giving 2, 4, 4, 5 and 30. Summarise the corrected observations, using denominator n for descriptive variance.
cases.focus: Sensitivity of the mean, median and variance

fields.label: Corrected mean (days)
fields.hint: The corrected total is 45 across five admissions.

fields.label: Corrected median (days)
fields.hint: Reorder the corrected observations and choose the third.

fields.label: Corrected descriptive variance (days²)
fields.hint: Square deviations from the corrected mean and divide their sum by 5.

steps.title: Describe the original records
steps.text: Originally x̄=5, median=4 and descriptive variance=36/5=7.2 days².

steps.title: Recalculate after the correction
steps.text: The new mean is 45/5=9 days. The median remains 4 days; the changed value is still above the middle observation.

steps.title: Track the squared deviations
steps.text: About the new mean 9, the deviations are −7, −5, −5, −4 and 21. Their squared sum is 49+25+25+16+441=556. Descriptive variance is 556/5=111.2 days²; adjusted variance is 556/4=139 days².

steps.title: Keep context
steps.text: The mean and variance are sensitive to magnitude. Investigate whether 30 is a valid complex admission or a recording problem; neither the median’s stability nor an outlier flag justifies automatic deletion.

cases.reflection: Explain which summaries changed most and what you would do before removing the 30-day stay.
cases.model: The mean rises from 5 to 9 days and descriptive variance from 7.2 to 111.2 days², while the median stays at 4 days. The long record has a strong influence on summaries that use its magnitude. Verify the record and clinical context before deciding how to analyse or report it.
rubric: Compares original and corrected mean and median
Distinguishes squared variance units from days
Investigates the long stay rather than automatically deleting it
cases.trap: Variance is measured in days². Report SD, the square root of variance, if you need a spread in days.

cases.title: A probability model for follow-up visits
cases.scenario: An illustrative model for next-month follow-up visits has X=0,1,2,3 with probabilities 0.10,0.40,0.30,0.20. Treat these as model probabilities, not observed sample frequencies.
cases.focus: Expected value, variance and a discrete tail

fields.label: Expected visits E(X)
fields.hint: Weight each possible visit count by its probability.

fields.label: Variance Var(X) (visits²)
fields.hint: Calculate E(X²) first, then subtract [E(X)]².

fields.label: Probability of at least 2 visits (decimal)
fields.hint: At least 2 includes both 2 and 3.

steps.title: Validate the model
steps.text: All probabilities are nonnegative and their sum is 1. The possible counts are discrete; there is no outcome of 1.6 visits for a single person.

steps.title: Weight outcomes
steps.text: E(X)=0×0.1+1×0.4+2×0.3+3×0.2=1.6 visits. This is a long-run average, not the most likely outcome.

steps.title: Choose the tail
steps.text: P(X≥2)=P(X=2)+P(X=3)=0.5. Here P(X>2)=0.2, so a strict versus inclusive inequality matters.

excel.label: Expected value, counts A2:A5 and probabilities B2:B5
Second moment, squared counts in C2:C5

cases.reflection: Explain why expected visits can equal 1.6 and why P(X≥2) differs from P(X>2).
cases.model: The expectation is the probability-weighted long-run average of visit counts and need not be an individual outcome. In this discrete model, “at least 2” includes the mass at 2, giving 0.5; “more than 2” includes only 3, giving 0.2.
rubric: Describes expectation as a weighted long-run average
Recognises that one patient has an integer visit count
Includes the probability mass at 2 for the inclusive tail
cases.trap: An unweighted average of the four possible counts would ignore how likely each outcome is.
cases.source: Topic 2, slides 1–64; Exercise Book 2026/27, exercises 13–28; Statistical Tables, tables D.1 and D.2.

cases.title: Translate a normal waiting-time question
cases.scenario: For an illustrative planning model, an individual waiting time X is normal with mean 30 minutes and SD 6 minutes. Find the probability above 39 minutes, the probability between 24 and 39 minutes, and the 95th percentile. Evaluate whether a normal model is plausible before using it with real waiting-time data.
cases.focus: Tail direction, cumulative areas and inverse probability

fields.label: P(X > 39), decimal
fields.hint: 39 is 1.5 SD above 30; take one minus the cumulative probability.

fields.label: P(24 < X < 39), decimal
fields.hint: Standardise both boundaries: −1 and 1.5.

fields.label: 95th percentile (minutes)
fields.hint: Start from the standard-normal 0.95 percentile, then undo standardisation.

steps.title: Standardise individuals
steps.text: z(39)=(39−30)/6=1.5 and z(24)=(24−30)/6=−1. This question concerns individuals, so use SD=6, not a standard error.

steps.title: Subtract cumulative areas
steps.text: P(24<X<39)=Φ(1.5)−Φ(−1)≈0.7745375, about 77.45%. For this continuous model, including an endpoint does not change the probability.

steps.title: Reverse the operation
steps.text: z0.95≈1.644854, so x0.95=30+6×1.644854≈39.8691 minutes. This is a percentile of individual waits, not a confidence limit for the mean.

cases.reflection: Describe the 95th percentile in words and explain how it differs from a 95% confidence interval.
cases.model: Under the stated normal model, about 95% of individual waits are at or below 39.87 minutes. This cutoff describes the distribution of individual waits; a confidence interval would instead describe uncertainty about a population parameter estimated from sample data.
rubric: Identifies individuals and minutes
Explains the cumulative 95% cutoff
Separates a distribution percentile from parameter uncertainty
cases.trap: NORM.S.DIST(z,FALSE) returns a density height, not the area needed for these probabilities.
cases.source: Topic 2, slides 1–64; Exercise Book 2026/27, exercises 13–28; Statistical Tables, tables D.1 and D.2.

cases.title: A patient and a sample mean are different
cases.scenario: Assume independent systolic blood-pressure measurements from a normal population with mean 120 mmHg and SD 15 mmHg. Draw n=25 patients. Compare the probability that their sample mean exceeds 126 mmHg with the probability that one individual exceeds 126 mmHg.
cases.focus: Sampling distributions and the SD/SE distinction

fields.label: SE of the sample mean (mmHg)
fields.hint: Divide the population SD by √25.

fields.label: P(X̄ > 126), decimal
fields.hint: The sample-mean threshold is 2 standard errors above 120.

fields.label: P(X > 126), decimal
fields.hint: The individual threshold is only 0.4 standard deviations above 120.

steps.title: Identify two random variables
steps.text: X represents one individual measurement. X̄ represents the average of 25 independent measurements. They share expected value 120 but do not share spread.

steps.title: Find the sampling spread
steps.text: SE(X̄)=15/√25=3 mmHg, while SD(X)=15 mmHg. Normality of X makes the normal sampling distribution exact even though n<30.

steps.title: Explain precision
steps.text: An average smooths independent individual variation. Raising n to 100 would halve SE to 1.5 mmHg but would leave individual SD at 15 mmHg; it would not cure sampling bias.

cases.reflection: Why does the mean exceed 126 much less often? What changes if sample size increases?
cases.model: The sample mean has SE=3 mmHg, so 126 is two standard errors above its expectation. For an individual it is only 0.4 SD above the mean. Larger independent samples narrow the sampling distribution of averages; they do not make individual blood pressures less variable.
rubric: Uses SE for X̄ and SD for X
Compares the correct probabilities
Explains larger n without claiming reduced individual variability
cases.trap: The CLT is about the distribution of summaries. In this case the normal population already supplies an exact normal distribution for X̄.
cases.source: Topic 3, slides 1–33; Understanding Notation; Exercise Book 2026/27, exercises 29–32.

cases.title: Why one denominator changes the estimate
cases.scenario: Four illustrative independent observations are 4, 6, 8 and 10 minutes. Compute the descriptive variance, adjusted variance estimate and estimated SE of the mean. You are estimating spread, not performing a variance hypothesis test.
cases.focus: Degrees of freedom and estimator versus estimate

fields.label: Descriptive variance vₙ (minutes²)
fields.hint: The mean is 7 and the squared-deviation sum is 20; divide by 4.

fields.label: Adjusted variance s² (minutes²)
fields.hint: Divide the same squared-deviation sum by n−1.

fields.label: Estimated SE of the mean (minutes)
fields.hint: Take √s², then divide by √4.

steps.title: Calculate deviations
steps.text: x̄=7, so deviations are −3,−1,1,3 and their sum is zero. Squared deviations sum to 9+1+1+9=20 minutes².

steps.title: Choose the target
steps.text: The observed descriptive variance is 20/4=5 minutes². To estimate population variance with the course adjustment, s²=20/3≈6.666667 minutes².

steps.title: Estimate mean uncertainty
steps.text: s=√(20/3)≈2.581989 minutes and estimated SE=s/√4≈1.290994 minutes. Neither s nor SE is a variance.

steps.title: Interpret unbiasedness
steps.text: Under independent identically distributed sampling, S² is unbiased across repeated samples for σ². This does not mean the single realised estimate 6.666667 must equal the unknown population variance, and √S² is not generally unbiased for σ.

cases.reflection: Explain n−1 without claiming that the adjusted variance is always exactly correct.
cases.model: Estimating the mean from these same four observations forces their deviations to sum to zero, leaving three degrees of freedom. The n−1 adjustment corrects average bias in variance estimation across independent samples. This one estimate still varies from sample to sample.
rubric: Links the zero-sum deviations to three degrees of freedom
Explains repeated-sample rather than guaranteed accuracy
Distinguishes adjusted variance, SD and SE
cases.trap: Use STDEV.S, not VAR.S, in s/√n. The unit of SE should match the original measurement.
cases.source: Topic 3, slides 1–33; Understanding Notation; Exercise Book 2026/27, exercises 29–32.

cases.title: A small-sample interval for a mean score
cases.scenario: A random sample of 16 independent eligible patients has a quantitative score mean of 54 points and adjusted SD 8 points. Assume the population scores are approximately normal and population variance is unknown. Construct a 95% confidence interval for the population mean.
cases.focus: Unknown σ, t reference and margin versus width

fields.label: Margin of error (points)
fields.hint: SE=8/√16; multiply it by the t0.975 critical value with df=15.

fields.label: 95% CI lower endpoint (points)
fields.hint: Subtract the margin from 54.

fields.label: 95% CI upper endpoint (points)
fields.hint: Add the margin to 54.

steps.title: Choose t
steps.text: The SD of 8 is estimated from the sample. Use t with n−1=15 degrees of freedom, given the normality and independence assumptions.

steps.title: Find uncertainty
steps.text: SE=8/√16=2 points. For 95% confidence, α=0.05 and the cumulative critical percentile is 0.975. t15,0.975≈2.1314495.

steps.title: Build the interval
steps.text: Margin=2.1314495×2≈4.2628991 points. The interval is 54±4.2628991=[49.7371,58.2629] points. Its full width is 8.5258 points.

steps.title: Explain the level
steps.text: This estimates the eligible population’s mean score. The method has 95% repeated-sampling coverage under the stated model; the interval does not contain 95% of patient scores.

cases.reflection: Write an interval interpretation and explain why using 1.96 here would give a different interval.
cases.model: We estimate the mean score in the eligible patient population to be between 49.74 and 58.26 points using a 95% t procedure under independent normal sampling. The t critical value allows for estimating population SD; substituting 1.96 gives a narrower z interval that does not use the stated small-sample unknown-variance method.
rubric: Names the population mean and endpoints with units
Explains confidence as a property of the procedure
Justifies t with df=15 and an adjusted SD
cases.trap: The confidence level is 0.95, but the two-sided cumulative critical percentile is 0.975.
cases.source: Topic 4, slides 1–33; Formula Sheet; Exercise Book 2026/27, exercises 33–50.

cases.title: How many patients attend follow-up?
cases.scenario: A random sample of 250 independent eligible patients includes 175 who attend follow-up. Estimate the population attendance proportion with the course 95% Wald interval. Enter proportions and SEs as decimals, not percentages.
cases.focus: Observed-count checks and a proportion interval

fields.label: 95% CI lower endpoint (decimal)
fields.hint: Subtract the normal 0.975 cutoff times the estimated SE from 0.7.

fields.label: 95% CI upper endpoint (decimal)
fields.hint: Add the same margin to 0.7.

steps.title: Define success and target
steps.text: Success means attending follow-up. The observed estimate is p̂=175/250=0.7; the target π is the proportion among all eligible patients.

steps.title: Check observed counts
steps.text: There are 175 observed successes and 75 failures. Both exceed the course minimum of 5 and the common stricter guideline of 10.

steps.title: Translate to percentages
steps.text: The attendance estimate is 70%, with an approximate 95% interval of 64.32%–75.68% for the population proportion. The margin is about 5.68 percentage points, not 5.68% relative growth.

cases.reflection: Write the result as percentages and say which counts justify the approximation.
cases.model: The sample attendance estimate is 70%; the approximate 95% Wald interval estimates the population proportion as 64.32%–75.68%. The normal approximation is supported by 175 observed successes and 75 observed failures, given independent sampling. The interval’s confidence level refers to repeated-sampling coverage.
rubric: Uses percentages correctly without confusing them with proportions
Checks observed successes and failures
Identifies the population proportion and confidence procedure
cases.trap: For an interval use the observed p̂ in the SE. A proportion hypothesis test generally uses the null π₀ instead.
cases.source: Topic 4, slides 1–33; Formula Sheet; Exercise Book 2026/27, exercises 33–50.

cases.title: A decision close to the 5% cutoff
cases.scenario: A random sample of 25 independent patients has a mean pulse of 84 bpm. Assume a normal population with known SD σ=10 bpm. Test H₀: μ=80 against Hₐ: μ≠80 at a pre-specified α=0.05.
cases.focus: Known-σ z test and unrounded decisions

fields.label: Null SE (bpm)
fields.hint: Population SD is known: divide 10 by √25.

fields.label: Observed z statistic
fields.hint: Subtract the null mean 80 from 84 and divide by SE.

fields.label: Two-sided p-value (decimal)
fields.hint: Find 2×P(Z≥|z|).

steps.title: Set the question before testing
steps.text: The parameter is the eligible population’s mean pulse. The two-sided hypotheses compare μ with 80 bpm; α=0.05 is fixed before examining the result.

steps.title: Standardise under H₀
steps.text: Known σ and normal independent sampling justify z. SE₀=10/√25=2 bpm; z=(84−80)/2=2.

steps.title: Calculate the evidence
steps.text: p=2[1−Φ(2)]≈0.04550026. The 5% two-sided critical value is 1.959964, so |z| exceeds it and p<0.05. Retain precision until making the decision.

steps.title: Cross-check and interpret
steps.text: The matching 95% z CI is 84±1.959964×2≈[80.0801,87.9199] bpm, excluding 80. Reject H₀ at 5%, with an estimate above 80. A 4 bpm difference still needs clinical context.

cases.reflection: Write the conclusion without saying the null has a 4.55% probability of being true.
cases.model: Under H₀ and the normal independent-sampling model, a result at least as extreme in either direction as z=2 has probability about 0.0455. Reject H₀ at 5%; the data provide evidence that the population mean differs from 80 bpm, with an estimated mean of 84 bpm. The p-value does not give the probability that H₀ is true.
rubric: States hypotheses about μ and the pre-specified 5% level
Uses the unrounded p-value to reject
Interprets evidence without assigning a probability to H₀ or claiming clinical importance
cases.trap: Rounding 0.0455 to 0.05 can obscure the decision. Compare the unrounded result with α.
cases.source: Topic 5, slides 1–36 (reviewed 7 October 2026); Formula Sheet; Exercise Book 2026/27, exercises 51–60; mock-answer document Q7–Q9. The guide uses the current book numbering; the slide exercise ranges are older. Type II error/power and the proportion counterexample are clearly labelled supplementary context.

cases.title: A higher observed proportion may be inconclusive
cases.scenario: Among 300 randomly sampled independent eligible adults, 192 support a health programme. Test H₀: π=0.60 against Hₐ: π≠0.60 at a pre-specified α=0.05, using the course normal approximation without continuity correction.
cases.focus: Null-based SE and a careful non-rejection

fields.label: Observed proportion p̂ (decimal)
fields.hint: Divide 192 by 300.

fields.label: Observed z statistic
fields.hint: Use SE₀=√(0.60×0.40/300), then standardise p̂−0.60.

fields.label: Two-sided p-value (decimal)
fields.hint: Use twice the normal upper tail beyond |z|.

steps.title: Check the model under H₀
steps.text: Expected null successes are 300×0.6=180 and failures 120. Both are ample for the course approximation. The observed support estimate is 192/300=0.64.

steps.title: Make the decision
steps.text: Two-sided p≈0.1572992, greater than 0.05. Do not reject H₀. The observed proportion is higher than 0.60, but this test does not provide sufficient evidence of a population difference at 5%.

steps.title: Keep claims bounded
steps.text: Non-rejection is not proof that π=0.60. The 4-percentage-point observed excess is an effect estimate; its sign alone does not determine significance.

cases.reflection: Explain the observed excess and the 5% decision in one short paragraph.
cases.model: The sample support proportion is 64%, which is 4 percentage points above the null value of 60%. The null-based two-sided z test gives p≈0.1573, so we do not reject at 5%. This result is insufficient evidence of a population difference at that level; it does not prove equality.
rubric: Reports 64% and a 4-percentage-point excess
Uses the null SE and p≈0.1573 to decide
Avoids claiming the population proportion is proven equal to 60%
cases.trap: A numerical difference between p̂ and π₀ is expected under sampling variation. It is not by itself a test decision.
cases.source: Topic 5, slides 1–36 (reviewed 7 October 2026); Formula Sheet; Exercise Book 2026/27, exercises 51–60; mock-answer document Q7–Q9. The guide uses the current book numbering; the slide exercise ranges are older. Type II error/power and the proportion counterexample are clearly labelled supplementary context.

cases.title: Compare two independent clinic means
cases.scenario: Independent random clinic samples have n₁=144, mean₁=12 minutes, adjusted SD₁=6 minutes; n₂=100, mean₂=15 minutes, adjusted SD₂=5 minutes. Assume well-behaved sampling distributions. Use the course large-sample normal approximation for H₀: μ₁−μ₂=0 at 5%. Topic 6 is additional, time permitting.
cases.focus: Contrast direction and adding independent variances

fields.label: Estimated clinic 1 − clinic 2 difference (minutes)
fields.hint: Keep the requested order: 12−15.

fields.label: Observed z statistic
fields.hint: Divide the estimated difference by its SE.

steps.title: Define the contrast
steps.text: Δ=μ₁−μ₂ in minutes, so the observed estimate is 12−15=−3. Different patients in the two clinics make this an independent comparison, given the stated design.

steps.title: Add sampling variances
steps.text: SE=√(36/144+25/100)=√(0.25+0.25)=√0.5≈0.7071068 minutes. Each group uses its own n and adjusted SD.

steps.title: Test and attach uncertainty
steps.text: z=−3/0.7071068≈−4.242641. Two-sided normal p≈0.00002209. The 95% large-sample CI is about [−4.3859,−1.6141] minutes.

steps.title: Explain direction, not causation
steps.text: Reject equal means at 5%. Clinic 1’s estimated population mean is 3 minutes lower. An observational comparison cannot establish that the clinic itself caused the difference; patient mix may matter.

cases.reflection: Interpret the negative contrast and describe what reversing group order would change.
cases.model: Clinic 1 has an estimated mean wait 3 minutes lower than clinic 2, with a large-sample 95% CI from about 1.61 to 4.39 minutes lower. Reversing the contrast reverses the estimate and interval signs, leaving SE and the two-sided p-value unchanged. An observed group difference alone does not establish a causal clinic effect.
rubric: Reports the contrast in the specified order with minutes
Explains reversed signs but unchanged SE and two-sided p
Separates observational association from a causal explanation
cases.trap: Do not add SDs or use s/√(n₁+n₂). Independence makes the variances of the two sample means add.
cases.source: Topic 6, slides 1–29; Exercise Book 2026/27, exercises 61–64. Additional topic in the syllabus, time permitting.

cases.title: An interval that includes zero
cases.scenario: Two independent random samples of quantitative patient scores have n₁=64, mean₁=45, adjusted SD₁=8; n₂=100, mean₂=47, adjusted SD₂=10. Assume well-behaved large-sample means and use the course normal approximation at 5%. Topic 6 is additional, time permitting.
cases.focus: Non-rejection, interval uncertainty and practical importance

fields.label: Two-sided p-value (decimal)
fields.hint: Difference=−2 and SE=√(64/64+100/100)=√2; calculate the two-sided normal tail.

steps.title: Keep the group order
steps.text: The estimated mean contrast is 45−47=−2 points. Scores vary within each group; the target is a difference of population means, not a difference for every patient.

steps.title: Compute uncertainty
steps.text: SE=√(8²/64+10²/100)=√2≈1.414214 points. The standardised contrast is −2/√2≈−1.414214.

steps.title: Read p and CI together
steps.text: Two-sided p≈0.1572992. The matching 95% normal CI is −2±1.959964×√2≈[−4.7718,0.7718] points. It includes zero, agreeing with non-rejection at 5%.

steps.title: Describe what remains plausible
steps.text: The estimated difference is below zero, but the interval also includes small positive values. Statistical non-rejection does not establish equivalence or absence of an important effect. Clinical importance needs a relevant effect threshold and study context.

cases.reflection: Comment on the estimate, p-value, interval and why “no difference” is too strong.
cases.model: The estimated mean contrast is −2 points, with p≈0.1573 and a 95% interval [−4.77,0.77] points. We do not reject equal population means at 5%. The interval includes zero and differences in both directions, so this is uncertainty rather than proof of no difference, equivalence or lack of clinical importance.
rubric: Reports −2 points and both interval limits
Connects p>0.05 and inclusion of zero to non-rejection
Distinguishes non-rejection from equivalence and clinical conclusions
cases.trap: An interval spanning zero is not an equivalence test. Do not replace “insufficient evidence” with “the treatments are identical”.
cases.source: Topic 6, slides 1–29; Exercise Book 2026/27, exercises 61–64. Additional topic in the syllabus, time permitting.
